newsitem.title: RUSSIA: IMF official says Russia can keep economy on track.
newsitem.headline: IMF official says Russia can keep economy on track.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund believes Russia can resolve the budget problems which led to a delay in paying part of a $10 billion loan, the IMF's top official in Russia said on Wednesday.

An IMF team monitoring Russia's economic performance left earlier this month without making a recomendation on whether to pay the latest $330 million tranche. The delegation was worried over the low level of tax collection in Russia.
But IMF resident representative Thomas Wolf told an international investment conference that the Russian authorities were taking the problem seriously.

"The IMF is convinced that, with continued determined efforts on the part of the authorities to solve the revenue problem and get revenues back up, this situation of financial stabilisation, which has basically been achieved, can be consolidated in the coming weeks and months," Wolf said. The IMF team is due to return for more talks with Russian authorities in mid-November.

Wolf said that by IMF methods of calculation, federal budget revenues had fallen to 8.5-9 percent of gross domestic product in the first nine months of 1996 from about 16.5 percent in 1992. Under a 1995 standby agreement with the IMF, budget revenues should have been 13.5 percent of GDP.

"Just think what could be done with respect to the social programmes which are underfunded, with respect to state investment in infrastructure...and also in terms of reducing further the budget deficit," he said.
Wolf described as "quite remarkable" the reduction in monthly inflation from about 18 percent in January 1995 to an average zero in August and September 1996.
But unemployment had doubled to more than nine percent, by International Labour Organisation methods, since the end of 1992 and there was also a lot of underemployment in Russian firms.
"As the restructuring process continues...it can only reasonably be expected that unemployment will rise further before it starts to fall," Wolf said.
